body:
Why western India's trade routes mattered

Ancient and early-medieval Gujarat was connected to both inland and maritime commerce. Its western coastline opened routes across the Arabian Sea, while inland roads linked commercial settlements to Malwa, Rajasthan and the Deccan.

These connections mattered politically because control over productive land, towns and trading routes could increase a ruler's access to resources. Commercial activity also brought travellers, merchants and religious communities into contact with one another.

Trade during the Western Kshatrapa period

During the early centuries CE, Bharukachchha or Bharuch was a prominent western trading outlet. Ujjain in Malwa was an important inland centre connected with long-distance routes.

The circulation of Western Kshatrapa silver coins is evidence of a developed monetary economy. Rulers could benefit from commerce and the movement of goods, although a coin found at a particular place does not necessarily prove that the issuing ruler directly governed that place.

Trade during the Maitraka period

By the middle of the 1st millennium CE, Vallabhi had become an important commercial centre under the Maitrakas. Its position in Saurashtra linked it with the trading activity of the western coast and the surrounding hinterland.

The Sanskrit literary work Dashakumaracharita, associated with Dandin, presents Vallabhi as a prosperous city connected with wealthy sea-traders. This literary association is consistent with the commercial importance of Vallabhi during the period.

Vallabhi was not simply another name for Bharuch. Bharuch had a major history as a coastal trading outlet, while Vallabhi became an important Maitraka capital, commercial town and centre of learning. Their importance belongs to overlapping but distinct regional developments.

The different historical contributions

Western Kshatrapas

The Western Kshatrapas are especially important for the political history of Shaka rule in western India, the use of Kshatrapa and Mahakshatrapa titles, long-running coinage, competition with the Satavahanas and Rudradaman's record of the Sudarshana Lake restoration.

Rudradaman's Sanskrit inscription is particularly significant because it demonstrates the use of elaborate Sanskrit royal praise under a Shaka ruler. It also gives precise information about irrigation works and provincial administration in Gujarat.

Maitrakas

The Maitrakas are especially important for the development of an early-medieval regional kingdom centred on Vallabhi. Their Sanskrit copper-plate grants illuminate administration, rural resources and the support of religious institutions.

Vallabhi's association with Buddhist learning, the comparison with Nalanda and its place in Shvetambara Jain literary tradition make it one of the significant cultural centres of early-medieval Gujarat.

Distinguishing similar names and sources

  • Chandragupta Maurya: The Sudarshana Lake was originally constructed during his reign by the governor Pushyagupta.
  • Chandragupta II: The Gupta ruler who defeated the last Western Kshatrapas around the end of the 4th century CE.
  • Rudradaman I: Western Kshatrapa ruler associated with the Sanskrit Junagadh inscription and the repair of Sudarshana Lake.
  • Skandagupta: Gupta emperor associated with another repair of the same lake in the 5th century CE.
  • Bhatarka: Founder of the Maitraka line, whose early title was senapati.
  • Dhruvasena II: Maitraka ruler of Vallabhi associated with the period of Xuanzang's visit.
  • Xuanzang: Chinese pilgrim who visited Vallabhi around 640 CE.
  • Yijing: Chinese scholar who later recognised Vallabhi and Nalanda as major centres of learning.

Identify the source before identifying the dynasty

Junagadh Sanskrit rock inscription, approximately 150 CE: Think of Rudradaman, the Western Kshatrapas and Sudarshana Lake.

Vallabhi Sanskrit copper-plate grant: Think of Maitraka administration, land grants and religious endowments.

Xuanzang and Yijing: Think of the importance of Vallabhi as a Buddhist learning centre.

One-glance historical connections

The 2 ruling traditions show different aspects of Gujarat's history. The Western Kshatrapas illustrate political competition, trade, coinage and the management of irrigation works in the early centuries CE. The Maitrakas illustrate the rise of regional kingship, the use of land grants and the development of religious and educational institutions during the early-medieval period.

Prelims focus

  • Western Kshatrapas: Shaka rulers; important names include Nahapana, Chastana and Rudradaman.
  • Rudradaman: Junagadh inscription, approximately 150 CE, Sudarshana Lake restoration.
  • Chandragupta II: Defeated the last Western Kshatrapas.
  • Maitrakas: Regional rulers of Vallabhi from the late 5th to later 8th century CE.
  • Vallabhi: Associated with Maitraka copper plates, Buddhist learning and Jain literary tradition.
  • Bharukachchha: Ancient Bharuch, a major western trading outlet.
  • Trap: Chandragupta Maurya and Chandragupta II belong to different dynasties and different periods; their associations with Gujarat are not interchangeable.

[NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 35–38 and 42–44; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts-I, New Empires and Kingdoms, printed p. 114; e-PG Pathshala, Indian Numismatics, Western Kshatrapa Coinage: An Introduction, sections 1–4; Himanshu Prabha Ray, Contested Sea Spaces: Of Piracy and Sea Battles Along the West Coast of India, in Bridging the Gulf: Maritime Cultural Heritage of the Western Indian Ocean, 2016, printed pp. 133–134; Annette Schmiedchen, Maitrakas, The Encyclopedia of Ancient History: Asia and Africa, first published 2021; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Trade, Cultural Connections and the Key Distinctions Between the Two Dynasties
